title: Choose the visual world for brickbot.ro
question: The roll dealt the Substation Plate direction. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: Substation Plate
options.lineage: Romanian high-voltage signage, enamel rating plates and lockout tags
options.thesis: The team presented the way electrical equipment presents itself: riveted plates that state type, rating and origin, no adjectives.
options.viewport: A full-bleed photo of the team at Nationals with a yellow enamel rating plate bolted over the lower left (TEAM No. 15996 · EST. 2016 · FOCȘANI · RATED: WORLDS DIVISION FINALIST 2026). The Support action hangs off it as a lockout tag.
options.risk: Can tip into caution-tape cliché if the hazard stripes spread. The plates must carry facts, not decoration.

raised.raise: The current is simulated, not drawn. A real canvas arc runs along each plate edge and follows the pointer.
Two-ink economy. The UI is black and enamel yellow only; burgundy is reserved for one band, and photos stay full colour.
A fixed reading order. Every plate reads TYPE → RATING → ACTION, so a stranger scans the page like a panel.
Fixed regions. Plates sit on one bolt grid and the regions never move between breakpoints, they only stack.

options.label: Terrace Kit
options.lineage: the team's yellow-and-burgundy jerseys, knitted scarves and terrace tifo
options.thesis: BrickBot as the club strangers end up supporting: the website as the terrace, wearing the kit.
options.viewport: A knitted scarf band reading BRICKBOT 15996 crosses the screen over the Nationals celebration photo. A giant shirt number and the Support button sit on the scarf.
options.risk: The most familiar route: it can read like a football club, and the robot gets upstaged by the fans.

options.label: Silkscreen Loft
options.thesis: Every season pulled as an edition: team and robot printed off-register in yellow and burgundy on black.
options.viewport: A rack of repeated prints of the Nationals photo, each pulled in a shifted ink, with the headline silkscreened across it.
options.case: Fuses with real teen energy and is memorable to strangers. It loses on clarity: an edition grid hides the offer and the robot.
options.risk: Pop-art pastiche if the repeats aren't tied to real seasons.

options.label: Gravity-Rain Garden
options.viewport: A dusk garden with rain falling in several directions.
options.case: Fuses poorly: sponsors don't identify with a dream garden, and it says nothing about robots.
options.kept: Real simulation as web leverage: the current is computed, not painted.

options.label: One-Bit Desktop
options.thesis: The team as windows on a dithered desktop.
options.viewport: Overlapping windows of team facts on a dither ground.
options.case: Fuses as retro novelty that a national sponsor wouldn't read as serious.
options.kept: Strict ink economy: two inks do every job.

options.label: Night-Flight Six-Pack
options.thesis: Impact shown as six calm gauges.
options.case: Fuses poorly: the impact numbers don't exist yet, and gauges would make them up.

options.label: PC-98 Field
options.thesis: Fixed screen regions in pixel art.
options.viewport: Pixel artwork with a text window docked low.
options.case: Fuses as costume. It has no tie to Romanian robotics.

options.label: Silk Canopy Chords
options.case: Fuses poorly: the palette fights the brand, and the light ground fights dark-first.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A dark robotics-team site done well: big photo hero, stats row, latest season, sponsor strip.
canonCard.viewport: A full-bleed photo, a headline with two buttons, and a stats row under it.
canonCard.risk: Looks like every other FTC team site, which is the problem the brief named.
